newsitem.title: UK: British MP set to propose fox-hunting ban.
newsitem.headline: British MP set to propose fox-hunting ban.

text.p: A British Labour member of parliament set the stage on Monday for a mighty clash between the House of Commons and the House of Lords, the unelected upper chamber of parliament, by pledging to introduce an anti-hunting bill.

The new Labour government promised in its manifesto for last month's election to allow a free vote -- letting MPs follow their consciences instead of a party line -- on whether hunting stags and foxes with hounds should be banned.
But Prime Minister Tony Blair had hoped to delay any vote, fearing stubborn resistance from pro-hunting aristocrats in the House of Lords would impede more important legislation.

However, Labour MP Mike Foster, who came top of the annual ballot for a slot in the parliamentary timetable to introduce a measure of his choosing, confirmed on Monday that his bill would aim to outlaw hunting with hounds.

"Without giving the game away totally, it will definitely be to do with animal welfare - let's put it like that," Foster, who will give more details at a news conference later on Monday, told BBC radio.

Foster made clear that angling would not be included in his bill. "We're looking at wild mammals - so it's fox, deer, mink and hare - those are the four main groups we're looking at. Only hunting with dogs," he said.

The proposal is bound to be controversial and deeply unpopular in rural communities. Hunt "meets", a social occasion before the hunting starts, regularly attract protests from anti-hunting groups who also attempt to disrupt the chase, leading occasionally to violent clashes.
The British Field Sports Society has estimated that outlawing foxhunting would force most of Britain's 300 hunts to close, meaning the loss of as many as 33,000 jobs.

Farmers fear a ban, as well as ending the colourful sight of scarlet-coated riders and a pack of baying hounds in hot pursuit of a speeding fox, would make it impossible to keep down the fox population.

But animal rights groups say the practice is cruel and dispute that many jobs would be at risk. They say the hunts could take up drag-hunting, in which they race after hounds purusing an artificial scent rather than a fox.
Foster said he was braced for fierce opposition to his bill in the House of Lords, a bastion of the rich landowning classes for whom hunting has been a way of life for centuries.
"It's a tough fight and it's going to take 12, 18 months or more before anything can really come forward on this," he said.
